lesson.title: Everything on the Right Side: dict.values()
lesson.summary: The values() method returns a live view of every value stored in a dictionary, which is handy for totals, maximums, and other calculations that ignore the keys.
lesson.body:
If keys() gives you the labels in a dictionary, values() gives you the other half: everything stored under those labels, with the keys stripped away entirely. This matters whenever the calculation you want to do does not care what something is called, only what it is worth. Adding up every price in a cart, finding the highest temperature in a week of readings, or counting how many total items are in stock are all jobs for values(), not for the dictionary's keys.

Like keys(), the values() method returns a view object, dict_values, not a list. It is iterable and stays live if the dictionary changes later. Unlike keys, which can never repeat because every key in a dictionary is unique, values are allowed to repeat, since two different keys can easily be mapped to the same value.

temps = {"Mon": 68, "Tue": 71, "Wed": 65}
print(list(temps.values()))
print(sum(temps.values()))
print(max(temps.values()))

This prints [68, 71, 65], then 204, then 71. Wrapping values() in list() turns the view into an ordinary list for display. sum() adds the three temperatures directly, 68 plus 71 plus 65, giving 204, without you ever writing a manual loop. max() scans the same values and reports the largest one, 71, again with no loop of your own required. Both sum() and max() are built-in functions that happily accept any iterable, and a dict_values view counts as one.

A word of caution: values() throws away the connection between a value and its key. If you needed to know which day had the high temperature, not just what the high temperature was, values() alone cannot tell you. For that you need both the key and the value together, which is exactly what the items() method, coming up next, provides.
